01 · Data analyticsTableau project

Starbucks: what drives customer satisfaction and spend

Analysed 100,000 orders in a Kaggle dataset labelled Starbucks using Tableau Prep and three interactive dashboards. Exploratory findings included lower satisfaction for drive-thru than mobile app orders (3.44 vs 3.86) and about 12% higher spend among rewards members—not causal conclusions.

ChallengeWhich drivers of satisfaction and spend could a manager act on with limited time and money?
ApproachCleaned the data in Tableau Prep, built six views in three dashboards with click-to-filter actions, and checked every figure against the data.
DeliverableThree dashboards, a four-page case study and a dashboard walkthrough.
FindingsSatisfaction slips after about 5 minutes of waiting, the drive-thru scores lowest (3.44 against 3.86 for the mobile app), and rewards members spend about 12% more per order.

Exploratory associations, not evidence of causation. Read the full case study ↓

UX case study · team concept

TutorPay: designing for clearer tutor hours and payments

A research-led UX team concept for Rhodes University tutors who needed a clearer way to record work, understand how payments were calculated and raise payment queries.

Information Systems HonoursTeam project · 6 contributors
ContextUX coursework focused on tutor payments at Rhodes University.
PeopleStudent tutors working across modules and departments.
Core needLog work, verify pay, and know where to resolve a discrepancy.
OutputResearch artefacts, storyboards and refined mobile wireframes.

The problem

The team’s research described tutors tracking hours informally, receiving combined payments without a clear per-module or task breakdown, and lacking an obvious route to question an error. Uncertain timing and unclear calculations also made budgeting harder.

Design goal

Explore a central place where tutors could record hours, review itemised earnings by department and task, and follow up on payment discrepancies.

01 · DiscoverInterview tutors and map what they do, how and why.
02 · DefineSynthesise needs, persona, point of view and How Might We questions.
03 · ExploreSketch the service and build paper/mobile wireframe flows.
04 · Test & refineUse think-aloud feedback to improve navigation, forms and transparency.

Research & design approach

  • Discovery: three tutor interviews using a structured interview guide.
  • Synthesis: What–How–Why table, empathy map, needs and insights.
  • Framing: a project persona (“Fiona”), point-of-view statement and prioritised How Might We questions.
  • Prototype: storyboard and paper/mobile wireframes for account access, logging hours, checking pay and reporting a discrepancy.
  • Evaluation: think-aloud user testing of the paper prototype, followed by documented design refinements.

What changed after testing

  • Added a visible “Log hours” action, consistent bottom navigation and clearer back navigation.
  • Separated daily entries from monthly submission and added a confirmation step before submitting.
  • Reworked the pay view to show itemised earnings, department split, deductions and net pay.
  • Added a discrepancy-report flow with categories, optional supporting files and ticket status tracking.
  • Improved login guidance with an email-format hint, “Remember me” and password recovery.
Methods & artefacts used: tutor interviews, empathy mapping, persona and POV, How Might We ideation, storyboarding, paper prototyping, mobile wireframing and think-aloud testing. Software: no specific design software is named in the source report, so none is credited here.

Data analytics case study · Tableau

Shopify sales analysis: how evenly revenue is spread across categories, channels, payments and countries

I explored a Kaggle Shopify sales dataset in Tableau to answer a simple commercial question: where does the revenue come from? I built four views of total revenue and combined them in two dashboards. The clearest result is that revenue is spread remarkably evenly, with no single category, channel, payment method or country dominating.

Data60,000 orders and 17 fields from a Kaggle Shopify sales dataset, covering order date, product, price, discount, quantity, country, traffic source, payment method, shipping cost, rating, returns, revenue and profit.
ToolsTableau.
BuildFour views in two dashboards: Shopify Sales Performance Overview and Customer Insights.
MeasureTotal revenue of 59,645,936 (currency not stated in the dataset), summed from the revenue field.

What the data shows

  • Traffic source: Social Media 12,021,807, Direct 11,953,141, Paid Ads 11,939,378, Organic 11,907,665 and Email 11,823,944. The top source leads the lowest by about 1.7%.
  • Country: seven countries, from Australia (8,698,941, about 14.6% of revenue) down to the UK (8,372,019). The gap between first and last is about 3.9%.
  • Payment method: Apple Pay 20.30%, Debit Card 19.96%, Credit Card 19.95%, Cash on Delivery 19.90% and PayPal 19.89%.
  • Product category: seven categories, with Electronics highest at roughly 8.7M and Footwear lowest at roughly 8.35M (read from the chart).

What this means

  • No channel, market or payment method is carrying the business, so revenue does not depend heavily on any one of them.
  • The differences are small, so I would not reallocate budget on these views alone. They are a baseline, not a basis for strong decisions.
  • A split this even is unusual for real store data, so it is worth checking how the dataset was built before generalising from it.
  • The recommendations below follow from this: test before acting, and look beyond revenue.

How the views were built

  • Product category: ranked bars shaded by revenue.
  • Traffic source and country: ranked bars with value labels. The country view uses a top-10 filter, which shows all seven countries in the data.
  • Payment method: a pie showing each method’s percentage of total revenue, appropriate because there are only five parts.
  • One measure, total revenue, is used throughout so the four views can be compared directly.

Limits

  • Revenue is not profit. The data also holds profit, discount, return and rating fields that these views do not use, so a high-revenue segment is not necessarily the most profitable.
  • The views describe totals and do not show cause and effect.
  • Category figures are read from the chart, not from a data table, so they are approximate.
Recommendations

What I would do next

Based on the revenue views. Each one is a suggestion to test, not a proven fix.

For the store

  • Test before shifting budget. Social Media leads traffic sources by under 2%, which is too small to justify moving spend. Run a controlled test and compare cost per order across sources, using ad spend data I did not have.
  • Keep every payment option. Revenue is almost equally split across all five methods (19.9% to 20.3%), so none is a clear candidate to drop, including Cash on Delivery.
  • Treat the markets as one even portfolio. The seven countries are within about 4% of each other. Compare shipping cost and profit per country before choosing where to focus campaigns, and consider Australia as a first test market because it leads.
  • Review categories on profit, not revenue. Electronics leads and Footwear trails, but the spread is only about 4%. Check margin before promoting or cutting either.

For the analysis

  • Add profit. Chart profit and profit margin by category, country and traffic source, since revenue alone can hide unprofitable segments.
  • Add returns, discounts and ratings. Compare return rate and average rating by category and country, and see whether heavier discounting lifts revenue or only lowers margin.
  • Add a time trend. Chart revenue by order date to look for seasonality or growth that the totals hide.
  • Validate the data. A split this even is unusual for real store data. Check how the dataset was built, and rerun the views on a real store’s orders before acting on the results.

Data note: this is a third-party Kaggle dataset used for an academic analysis; it is not presented as data from a live store I operate. The comparisons are descriptive and do not establish that one factor caused a change in revenue.

Data analytics case study · Power BI

BMW global sales dashboard: dealerships track units sold, marketing spend does not

I built a one-page Power BI dashboard on a Kaggle BMW sales dataset to see which factors line up with units sold. The headline result is a contrast: the number of dealerships in a market moves closely with units sold, while marketing spend shows almost no relationship with them.

Data1,000 monthly records from 2015 to 2024, covering 10 countries, 10 models, 3 model families and 15 fields including price, marketing spend, dealership count, competition index, units sold and revenue.
ToolsPower BI Desktop, DAX and a custom JSON theme.
BuildFive KPI cards, three slicers (year, country, model) and five charts on a 16:9 page.
ChecksKPI card values checked against a separate calculation on the underlying CSV.

What the data shows

  • Headline figures: 633,192 units, 47.97bn revenue, an average selling price of 75,758 and 279.5M marketing spend, or 171.6 of revenue per marketing dollar.
  • Country: China leads with 77,488 units (12.2% share), followed by the UK (11.2%) and France (10.6%). The USA is lowest at 52,647 (8.3%).
  • Model: the X3 leads with 73,358 units and the iX is lowest with 51,067. By family, the X range (SUV) accounts for about 40% of units, sedans 31% and the i range (electric) 29%.
  • Dealerships: r = 0.87 with units sold, a strong positive link.
  • Marketing spend: r = 0.05 with units sold, essentially no link.

How to read the yearly trend

  • Units by year swing from 53,249 in 2016 to 76,157 in 2015, against an average of 63,300.
  • Those swings mostly follow how many records each year has (118 in 2015, 83 in 2016), because units per record stays within roughly 600 to 665 every year.
  • So the line reflects the structure of the dataset and should not be read as a real rise or fall in demand.
  • The dashboard annotates the line with the record count for this reason.
Recommendations

What I would do next

Based on the dashboard. Each one is a suggestion to test, not a proven fix.

For the business

  • Pilot dealership growth. The strong link with units suggests dealership coverage matters. Test it by expanding in one under-served market, such as the USA, and compare against a similar market without expansion.
  • Review marketing effectiveness. Spend barely relates to units, so ask what the budget is buying. Test shifting some of it to a market or channel and measure the result before cutting anything.
  • Use China as the benchmark market. It has the highest units and share, so study what it does differently before copying it elsewhere.
  • Weigh the model mix. SUVs are about 40% of units, so protect that range while looking at why the iX and X7 trail.

For the analysis

  • Add competition and engine type. Competition index and engine type are in the data but not charted, and may explain differences between markets.
  • Control for market size. Dealership count likely rises with market size, so test the link within a single country or segment.
  • Normalise the yearly view. Show units per record so the trend is not driven by record counts.
  • Check against real data. This is a synthetic practice dataset, so rerun the same views on real sales and marketing data before acting.

Data note: this is a synthetic third-party Kaggle dataset used for practice; it is not BMW internal data and its results should not be read as real BMW performance. The correlations are descriptive and do not show that dealerships cause sales or that marketing has no effect.

Data analytics case study · Tableau

Starbucks order analysis: exploring satisfaction and spending patterns

I explored a Kaggle dataset labelled Starbucks to examine how fulfilment time, order channel, customisation and rewards status relate to customer satisfaction and order spend. I prepared the data in Tableau Prep and built three interactive dashboards in Tableau.

Data100,000 orders, 14,988 customers, 500 stores, 1 January 2024 to 30 December 2025 (Kaggle).
ToolsTableau Prep, Tableau and Excel.
BuildSix views in three dashboards, with click-to-filter actions.
ChecksEvery dashboard figure checked against the underlying data.

What the data shows

  • Waiting time: satisfaction is about 3.72 under 5 minutes and falls to 3.41 at 9 minutes or more.
  • Order channel: Mobile App 3.86, In-Store Cashier 3.70, Kiosk 3.60, Drive-Thru 3.44. Store location differs by less than 0.05.
  • Customisations: satisfaction rises from 3.61 with none to 3.92 at seven. Drink category makes almost no difference (3.68 to 3.69).
  • Rewards: members spend $15.72 per order against $14.09, about 12% more. Customers aged 55 and over average about $13.06.

Recommendations and limits

  • Reduce long waits, starting with the drive-thru, and learn from what works in the mobile app.
  • Test prompting light personalisation, and focus on service rather than individual drinks.
  • Grow rewards membership, and look more closely at customers aged 55 and over.
  • Limits: these are associations, not causes. Results at the extremes rest on few orders (451 orders at seven customisations, 73 orders over ten minutes). Rewards status is recorded per order, so the comparison is between orders, not fixed groups of people.

Data note: this is a third-party Kaggle dataset used for an academic analysis; it is not presented as Starbucks internal company data. The comparisons are descriptive and do not establish that one factor caused a change in satisfaction or spending.

BPM case study · service-learning project

St Mary’s DCC: redesigning stakeholder communication processes

A three-person Business Process Management service-learning project with St Mary’s Development and Care Centre, completed through Rhodes University in September 2026. The team examined four processes, documented the current state and proposed improved process models and an SOP.

OrganisationSt Mary’s Development and Care Centre, a non-profit organisation.
Process ownerCentre Manager, with Office Administrator engagement.
ScopeDonor and funder communication, onboarding, raising grievances and disciplining employees.
OutputsAs-Is and To-Be models, process improvement report, SOP and final presentation.

What we found

  • Donor communication: no communication manual, and deadlines tracked in a spreadsheet and WhatsApp.
  • Discipline and grievances: cases stalled because the management committee meets only quarterly.
  • Onboarding: no structured induction for new leadership.

What we proposed

  • A stakeholder communication manual and a centralised donor database with reminders.
  • A monthly Executive Committee to unblock discipline and grievances.
  • Structured onboarding with a mentor, and Rhodes volunteers for donor newsletters.
Team contribution and scope: I was one of three team members (Kamva Ncula, Nsuku Gwebana and Chimwemwe Mwansa). The source materials do not allocate individual task ownership, so this portfolio describes the shared team deliverables rather than claiming sole responsibility. The recommendations are proposed future-state changes; they are not evidence of implemented or measured impact.

How the team worked

  • Applied the six-phase BPM lifecycle: process identification, discovery, analysis, redesign, implementation planning and monitoring.
  • Used stakeholder interviews and clarification workshops to understand the current process.
  • Applied process observation and the 5 Whys technique to explore causes of delays and gaps.
  • Created and reviewed As-Is and To-Be process models before documenting the proposed procedures.

Examples of proposed changes

  • Donor and funder communication: a standard communication manual and Salesforce NPSP CRM for donor records, reminders and reporting.
  • Onboarding: a structured leadership induction, team introductions and a designated mentor.
  • Grievances and discipline: clearer formal routes, delegated decision-making and a monthly Executive Committee to reduce quarterly bottlenecks.
  • Donor communications capacity: use Rhodes University volunteer students to support donor newsletters.

Proposed monitoring targets

  • Grievances: 100% acknowledged within 5 days and resolved within 30 days.
  • Onboarding: 100% of onboarding communication within 3 working days.
  • Donor and funder communication: a target of 90% or higher donor retention.
  • These figures are proposed performance indicators in the project materials, not achieved results.

Project status and learning

  • The project reached process analysis, redesign and documentation / handover; the supplied report identifies further activity clarification and process-owner verification as next steps.
  • No post-implementation performance data was supplied.
  • The work highlighted the importance of stakeholder engagement, clear ownership, reliable records and realistic improvements that fit a non-profit’s capacity.

Project evidence

Visuals from the St Mary’s DCC engagement and the organisation’s identity, included to give context to the team’s process-discovery work.
